title: Density — why a kilogram of feathers takes up so much more space
examTip: Always check your units. Examiners may give mass in grams and volume in cm³. They may want the answer in kg/m³. Know how to convert: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
introTips: A kilogram of feathers and a kilogram of iron have the same mass. But the feathers fill a room, and the iron fits in your hand.
Density is why steel ships can float. It is the shape and what is inside that matters, not just the material.
This topic links straight to the required practical. You will measure density in the lab.
intro: Why does wood float while a nail sinks, even if the nail is lighter? Why is a bag of flour much heavier than the same size bag of popcorn? The answer is density. Density measures how much mass is packed into a given volume. It is one of the most useful quantities in science. It tells you what things are made of. It predicts whether they will float. It explains why the air gets thinner the higher you go. The particle model explains well why different substances have different densities.

keyPoints.heading: What density is and why it matters
keyPoints.content: Density measures how much mass is packed into a given volume. The equation is: ρ = m / V Where: ρ = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³), m = mass (kg or g), V = volume (m³ or cm³) A substance with high density has particles that are heavier, more closely packed, or both. Some key densities: - Air: ~1.2 kg/m³ - Water: 1000 kg/m³ (1 g/cm³) - Ice: 917 kg/m³ (less than water — so ice floats) - Aluminium: 2700 kg/m³ - Iron: 7900 kg/m³ - Gold: 19,300 kg/m³ - Osmium (densest natural element): 22,590 kg/m³ Floating and sinking: compare the object with the fluid it is in. An object floats if it is less dense than the fluid. An object sinks if it is denser than the fluid. Ice (917 kg/m³) floats on water (1000 kg/m³). This is why icebergs float. It is also why lakes freeze from the top down. This keeps the water life below alive.
writeBullets: Density (ρ) = mass (m) ÷ volume (V). Unit: kg/m³ or g/cm³
High density — particles are heavier, more closely packed, or both
Water: 1000 kg/m³; Air: ~1.2 kg/m³; Iron: 7900 kg/m³; Gold: 19,300 kg/m³
An object floats if density < fluid density. It sinks if density > fluid density
Ice (917 kg/m³) is less dense than water (1000 kg/m³). So ice floats

keyTerms.def: Mass per unit volume — how much mass is packed into a given space. Symbol: ρ (rho). Unit: kg/m³
The density equation: density equals mass divided by volume

keyPoints.memTip: ρ = m/V. Think 'rho equals mass over volume'. Rearrange using the triangle: cover what you want, and the rest is the calculation.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to mix up mass and density. A large object can have low density, like a balloon. A small object can have high density, like a lead weight.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating density — worked examples
keyPoints.content: The density equation and its rearrangements: ρ = m/V   m = ρV   V = m/ρ Worked example 1 — will it float? A block of pine wood has mass 600 g and volume 1000 cm³. ρ = m/V = 600/1000 = 0.6 g/cm³ = 600 kg/m³ 600 kg/m³ < 1000 kg/m³ (water), so the wood floats. ✓ Worked example 2 — finding mass from density and volume A gold ring has volume 0.8 cm³. Density of gold = 19.3 g/cm³. m = ρV = 19.3 × 0.8 = 15.4 g Worked example 3 — unit conversion A substance has density 2.7 g/cm³. Convert to kg/m³. 2.7 g/cm³ × 1000 = 2700 kg/m³ (aluminium) Unit conversion rule: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ To convert g/cm³ → kg/m³: multiply by 1000 To convert kg/m³ → g/cm³: divide by 1000
writeBullets: ρ = m/V. It rearranges to m = ρV and V = m/ρ
Always check units. Use the same units all through a calculation
1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Multiply by 1000 to convert g/cm³ to kg/m³
To check floating, compare the density you worked out with the density of the fluid
If density < fluid density → floats. If density > fluid density → sinks

keyTerms.def: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Multiply by 1000 to convert g/cm³ to kg/m³

keyPoints.memTip: Use a formula triangle. Put ρ at the top, and m and V at the bottom. Cover what you want to find.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Unit conversion errors lose the most marks in density questions. Practise them on purpose.

keyPoints.heading: Measuring density in the lab (required practical)
keyPoints.content: There are three set-ups you need to know for the required practical: 1. Regular solid (e.g., cuboid or cylinder): - Measure its size with a ruler. For a cuboid: length, width and height. For a cylinder: radius and height - Work out the volume with a formula: V = l × w × h (cuboid) or V = πr²h (cylinder) - Measure the mass using a balance - Calculate: ρ = m/V 2. Irregular solid (e.g., a stone or lump of metal): - Measure the mass with a balance - Fill a eureka can (displacement can) with water up to the spout. Then lower the object in gently - Collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder. The volume of water displaced = the volume of the object - Or use a measuring cylinder. Record the water level, add the object, and record the new level. Subtract to find the volume - Calculate: ρ = m/V 3. Liquids: - Measure a known volume of liquid using a measuring cylinder - Measure the mass of the empty container, then with the liquid. Subtract to find the mass of the liquid alone - Calculate: ρ = m/V Sources of error: parallax error when reading the measuring cylinder. Not fully covering the object with water. Using a worn ruler.
writeBullets: Regular solid — measure its size with a ruler. Use a formula for the volume. Use a balance for mass
Irregular solid — find the volume by displacement, with a eureka can or measuring cylinder
Volume of displaced water = volume of the irregular object (Archimedes' principle)
Liquid — measure a known volume with a measuring cylinder. Find its mass with a balance
All methods: measure mass and volume separately, then use ρ = m/V
Sources of error: parallax, not fully covering the object, worn equipment

keyTerms.def: A displacement can filled to the brim — used to measure the volume of an irregular object by collecting the water it displaces
The volume of liquid pushed aside when an object is submerged — equals the volume of the object

keyPoints.memTip: Regular → ruler and formula. Irregular → water displacement.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exam questions often ask you to describe the method for an irregular object. Make sure you say you collect the displaced water, not just 'put it in water'.

keyPoints.heading: Density and states of matter
keyPoints.content: The particle model explains why the three states of matter have such different densities: Gases are far less dense than liquids and solids. This is because the particles are very far apart. Most of a gas is empty space. For example, air (~1.2 kg/m³) is about 800 times less dense than water (1000 kg/m³). Solids are usually denser than liquids of the same substance. This is because particles in a solid are packed more tightly. But there is a famous exception: Water is unusual: ice (917 kg/m³) is LESS dense than liquid water (1000 kg/m³). In ice, water molecules form a regular, open hexagonal lattice. Forces of attraction between the molecules hold it together. This open structure takes up MORE space than the jumbled arrangement in liquid water. This is why: - Ice floats on liquid water - Lakes freeze from the top down. Ice forms at the surface and insulates the water below - Water life can survive under ice in winter Comparing states: - Aluminium solid: 2700 kg/m³ - Liquid aluminium: ~2375 kg/m³ (slightly less dense, as particles are slightly further apart) - Aluminium vapour: far less dense (particles very spread out) The density of a liquid compared with its gas is typically about 1000:1.
writeBullets: Gases are far less dense than solids and liquids. They are mostly empty space between particles
Solids are usually denser than liquids of the same substance. Their particles are packed more tightly
Exception: Ice (917 kg/m³) is LESS dense than liquid water (1000 kg/m³)
Ice forms an open hexagonal lattice. This takes up more space than jumbled liquid water
Ice floats → lakes freeze from the top down → water life is protected under the ice
Liquid to gas density ratio: typically ~1000:1. For example, water and water vapour

keyTerms.def: The open ring-shaped structure of ice — water molecules held in a wider arrangement than in liquid water, making ice less dense

keyPoints.memTip: Most solids are denser than their liquid. But water is the exception. Ice floats, which shows solid water is LESS dense than liquid water.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The water and ice density exception is a favourite exam question. Make sure you can explain it using particle arrangement, not just state the fact.

0.question: A stone has a mass of 270 g and a volume of 100 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! ρ = m/V = 270/100 = 2.7 g/cm³. This is the density of aluminium. The stone is denser than water, so it sinks.
0.wrongFeedback: Use ρ = m/V. Divide mass by volume: 270 ÷ 100 = 2.7 g/cm³. Make sure you divide the right way round. Mass goes on top.

1.question: A metal block has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm3. What is its density?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. Density = mass / volume = 540 / 200 = 2.7 g/cm3. This is the density of aluminium. Always check your units. If mass is in g and volume in cm3, the density is in g/cm3.
1.wrongFeedback: Use the formula: density = mass / volume. Here: 540 g / 200 cm3 = 2.7 g/cm3. A common mistake is to multiply instead of divide. Check your units too. Mass in g and volume in cm3 gives density in g/cm3.

2.question: How would you measure the volume of an irregular lump of rock in the lab?
options: Put it in water in a eureka can or measuring cylinder. Measure the volume of water displaced
Measure its length, width and height with a ruler and multiply them together
Weigh it on a balance and divide by its known density
Place it on a measuring cylinder and read off the scale
2.correctFeedback: Spot on. For irregular objects you use water displacement. The volume of water pushed out equals the volume of the object.
2.wrongFeedback: You can only use length × width × height for regular shapes like cuboids. For irregular shapes, use water displacement. A eureka can or measuring cylinder gives you the volume directly.

3.question: Why does ice float on liquid water? Choose the best explanation.
options: Ice is less dense than liquid water. Its particles form an open hexagonal lattice that takes up more space
Ice is less dense. Its particles have less mass than liquid water particles
Ice floats because it is a solid and all solids float on liquids
Ice floats because it is colder and cold things are always less dense
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right. Ice forms an open hexagonal structure. Its particles are slightly further apart than in liquid water. That makes ice less dense (917 vs 1000 kg/m³).
3.wrongFeedback: Ice and liquid water are made of the same water molecules, with the same mass. The difference is how they are arranged. In ice, a hexagonal lattice makes a more open structure. So the same mass takes up more volume → lower density.

commonMistakes: Dividing volume by mass instead of mass by volume. Remember ρ = m/V, not V/m.
Forgetting to convert units. Mixing grams with m³, or cm³ with kg, gives nonsense answers. Use the same units all the way through.
Thinking all solids are denser than liquids. Ice is the classic exception: it is less dense than water.
Saying an object 'loses mass' when placed in water. It doesn't. The water displaced has the same volume as the object, not the same mass.
Forgetting to subtract the empty container's mass when finding a liquid's density.
examTips: In every density calculation, clearly show your formula, substitution and units. The mark scheme gives marks for each step.
If asked whether an object floats or sinks, work out its density. Compare it directly with the fluid's density, and say so clearly.
For the required practical, know the method for BOTH regular and irregular objects. Say which instrument measures which quantity.
